items.rawSummary: Iranian state media reported the draft nuclear agreement is in final ratification stages, while hardline officials reiterated demands for U.S. concessions and accused President Trump of fabricating deal terms, as the U.S. naval blockade continued.
items.analysis: Ceasefire diplomacy remained in flux as Iranian officials denied any finalized agreement and reiterated red lines, including no transfer of enriched uranium abroad and insistence on controlling the Strait of Hormuz. Hardline posturing intensified, with the parliamentary National Security Committee ruling out uranium transfers, a spokesperson demanding the U.S. Treasury Secretary ‘bow before Iran’s might,’ and Speaker Ghalibaf stating that Iran concedes not through dialogue but with missiles. Both Mohsen Rezaei and IRGC Commander Ahmad Vahidi warned Iran would break the blockade by negotiation or direct action if it persisted, while top negotiators expressed growing pessimism. Fars news agency later reported that the agreement had entered its final ratification stages but no final decision had been made, and accused President Trump of misrepresenting the draft deal, with informed sources describing his statements as a mix of truth and fabrication intended to claim premature victory. Fars asserted that the text does not stipulate the Strait of Hormuz opening freely or the dismantlement of nuclear materials, and that Iran demands the U.S. unblock $12 billion in assets and secure a ceasefire in Lebanon on Hezbollah’s terms before talks proceed. Trump advisor Stephen Miller acknowledged significant Iranian concessions, and the New York Times detailed a proposed $300 billion U.S.-facilitated investment fund, even as the naval blockade redirected 115 vessels and disabled four, while Ynet revealed that Mossad used Iranian recruits years earlier to disable a key air-defense site.

items.rawSummary: As the White House moves toward a final decision on lifting the naval blockade and dismantling Iran's buried enriched uranium, diplomatic channels widen with Pakistan's foreign minister meeting Secretary Rubio, while domestic developments include soaring debt interest costs and the arrest of a former CIA official.
items.analysis: U.S.-Iran negotiations have reached a critical juncture, with President Trump publicly laying out demands that include immediate toll-free transit through the Strait of Hormuz, an Iranian commitment never to possess nuclear weapons, lifting of the naval blockade, and U.S.-led extraction of buried enriched uranium in coordination with Iran and the IAEA, ahead of a Situation Room meeting to decide on the deal. Vice President Vance said Iran has agreed not to build or possess a nuclear program and is negotiating in good faith, while Treasury Secretary Bessent warned that kinetic military action could resume if no peace agreement is reached. Pakistan’s foreign minister met with Secretary of State Marco Rubio, with talks centered on brokering a permanent end to the conflict involving the U.S., Israel, and Iran. On the domestic front, interest costs on public debt hit a record $616 billion, a former CIA executive was arrested with 300 gold bars and a fabricated resume, and the White House launched and then redirected an aliens-themed website to an ICE arrest map.

items.title: Strait of Hormuz area (Bandar Abbas vicinity), Iran: Tehran announced that Foreign Minister Araghchi discussed a proposed "future management mechanism" for the Strait of Hormuz with Oman's foreign minister, citing sovereignty and international law.
items.description: Tehran announced that Foreign Minister Araghchi discussed a proposed "future management mechanism" for the Strait of Hormuz with Oman's foreign minister, citing sovereignty and international law.
items.rawSummary: The deadlock over a ceasefire and the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz continues as Tehran formally proposes a joint management mechanism with Oman, while naval confrontations and US sanctions keep the waterway tense and shipping anchors cautiously on the Omani side.
items.analysis: U.S. Vice President JD Vance indicated that Washington and Tehran are 'very close' to a memorandum of understanding that would extend a ceasefire, reopen the Strait of Hormuz, and launch nuclear talks, but the deadlock has persisted with small-scale naval confrontations in recent days and final approval from President Trump—and reportedly also from Iranian Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei—still pending, with Khamenei’s statements suggesting he will not cede Iranian control of the waterway. Iran’s dual strategy of seeking formal recognition while maintaining missile and drone threats is reflected in continued IRGC Navy warning shots and missile launches at vessels, even as the diplomatic track limps along. The U.S. has applied further pressure through Treasury sanctions on the Persian Gulf Strait Authority on May 27, warning against cooperation, and CENTCOM strikes aim to prevent Iran from establishing a protection racket in the strait; meanwhile, Gulf states are reportedly furious with Oman over its role in talks on joint management, viewing any Omani-Iranian arrangement as a direct threat. On May 29, Ebrahim Rezaei, spokesman for Iran’s parliamentary National Security Commission, claimed that the Islamic Republic’s authority over the Strait of Hormuz is recognized worldwide and that countries coordinate passage and pay fees for their vessels to transit, a direct assertion of the sort of control the U.S. and its allies have vowed to prevent. Multiple vessels were subsequently observed anchoring consecutively near the Omani side, indicating heightened shipping caution. That same day, Iranian Foreign Minister Araghchi spoke with Oman’s foreign minister to promote a 'future management mechanism' for the strait, citing sovereignty and international law—an overture that underscores Tehran’s push for a formal governing role even as the standoff grinds on.
